name: Aaron Bobick
milestone_by_age_26: No verified birth year found; MIT BS Math/CS 1981 and PhD cognitive science 1987 imply a typical late-20s doctorate. Major academic leadership (Georgia Tech School of Interactive Computing chair; WashU McKelvey Engineering dean from 2015) and public visibility arrived well after any plausible age-26 window. No dated material founder/engineering fame milestone by age 26 verified.
early_history_summary: MIT undergraduate degrees in mathematics and computer science (1981), then MIT PhD in cognitive science (1987). Early faculty path through MIT Media Lab and Georgia Tech GVU Center / School of Interactive Computing; later dean of WashU McKelvey Engineering.
evidence_summary: Career timeline is well documented via Wikipedia and institutional bios (MIT degrees 1981/1987; Media Lab; Georgia Tech; WashU dean 2015). Without a birth year, age at PhD cannot be confirmed ≤26; even if PhD were near 26, ordinary doctoral completion alone is not treated as a material fame milestone under this rubric. No dated founding, award, or field-defining product by age 26 found.

name: Urs Hölzle
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1964; ETH Zurich master's and Fulbright scholarship in 1988 (age ~24) are ordinary elite graduate credentials. Stanford PhD (1994, age ~30), Strongtalk/HotSpot JVM path, and joining Google as employee #8 / first VP of Engineering (1999, age ~35) all occurred after 26. No material dated founder/engineering fame milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Swiss-born computer scientist; CS master's from ETH Zurich (1988), Fulbright to the U.S., Stanford PhD on programming-language implementation (1994). Co-founded work that became HotSpot; later UCSB associate professor before joining Google in 1999 as early engineering leader for infrastructure and data centers.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and Google/career sources place birth in 1964 (Liestal, Switzerland), MS ETH 1988, PhD Stanford 1994, Google 1999. The career-defining infrastructure leadership and Google employee #8 role are mid-30s milestones. Pre-26 record is strong graduate education only.

name: Liz Fong-Jones
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1987; joined Google as systems administrator in 2008 (age ~21) and began internal organizing by ~2010–2011, but public fame and material industry impact arrived later (Never Again pledge 2016 age ~29; Damore memo / walkout leadership 2017–2018 ages ~30–31; Honeycomb Field CTO after 2019). Early Google employment alone is not treated as a career-defining milestone by age 26 under this rubric.
early_history_summary: Started Caltech in 2005, left in 2007 amid financial and transition pressures, then worked in MMO tech support and joined Google in 2008. Completed MIT EECS BS in 2014 while advancing as an SRE; became a leading Google labor/ethics organizer in the late 2010s before moving to Honeycomb.
family_context_summary: Family of engineers normalized tech; uncles taught early programming. Parents were not supportive of transition; biological father disowned her in her teens.
parent_family_domain_summary: Engineering relatives provided early computing access and domain fluency; not a formal industry pipeline into Google fame.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia documents birth year 1987, Google from 2008, MIT BS 2014, and public activism peak 2017–2019. Bloomberg and Fast Company profiles confirm early family engineering exposure and teen family rejection. The independently famous milestones (walkout fund, Project Maven/Dragonfly organizing, Honeycomb leadership) cluster after age 26.

name: Forrest Norvell
milestone_by_age_26: No verified birth year or dated material founder/engineering fame milestone by age 26 found. Known as npm CLI team lead / open-source Node engineer in the mid-2010s; public conference and podcast visibility is specialist community recognition without a clear ≤26 breakthrough.
early_history_summary: Open-source JavaScript/Node engineer; led npm CLI work and spoke on ES6/community topics (e.g., JSConf 2014). Later roles include New Relic and Arcjet engineering leadership. No Wikipedia biography or reliable early-life chronology located.
evidence_summary: Public footprint is GitHub (othiym23), npm-era talks/podcasts, and later Arcjet engineering roles. Without birth year or a dated ≤26 milestone backed by two sources, marked ineligible.

name: Estelle Weyl
milestone_by_age_26: No verified birth year; public bios place ~25 years of front-end experience and web-standards work from ~2000 (O'Reilly author, MDN contributor, Perf Matters organizer). People-search age estimates (~late 50s) would put 2000 well after age 26. No dated material milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Open Web evangelist and front-end engineer; transitioned into standards-focused web development around 2000. Consulted for Yahoo, Apple, Samsung and others; authored CSS/HTML books for O'Reilly and teaches widely.
evidence_summary: O'Reilly and personal site bios emphasize standards work from 2000 and long consulting/teaching career; no birth year or adolescent milestone documented. Ineligible under age-26 rule.

name: Ronald Baecker
milestone_by_age_26: In May–June 1969, at age 26, published the pioneering AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference paper 'Picture-Driven Animation' and completed his MIT PhD thesis 'Interactive Computer-Mediated Animation' (GENESYS), a landmark early interactive computer-animation system.
early_history_summary: Born October 7, 1942 in Kenosha, Wisconsin. Earned MIT physics BS (1963), electrical engineering MS (1964), and computer science PhD (1969) while developing interactive picture-driven animation (GENESYS). Later co-founded Toronto's Dynamic Graphics Project and became a leading HCI researcher and entrepreneur.
primary_leverage_engine: Scarce technical depth in early interactive graphics
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond birthplace (Kenosha, Wisconsin).
primary_early_advantage_tags: MIT, Project MAC, early computer graphics lab access, interactive animation, 1960s computing frontier
evidence_summary: Born 1942; MIT degrees through 1969 PhD are documented on Wikipedia and ACM bios. The 1969 SJCC 'Picture-Driven Animation' paper and June 1969 MIT LCS thesis establish a dated, field-recognized milestone at age 26 (before his October birthday). Access to MIT Project MAC-era interactive graphics hardware was a scarce era advantage. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born October 7, 1942 in Kenosha, Wisconsin; early life and family class context not documented in reviewed sources; entered MIT for undergraduate study in physics.
current_position: Emeritus Professor of Computer Science and former Bell Chair in Human-Computer Interaction at the University of Toronto; ACM Distinguished Speaker; author of recent books on ethical tech and digital society.

trajectory.event: Published 'Picture-Driven Animation' at AFIPS SJCC and completed MIT PhD thesis on interactive computer-mediated animation (GENESYS).
Joined University of Toronto faculty and helped build the Dynamic Graphics Project, a foundational Canadian HCI/graphics lab.
Co-authored the influential 'Readings in Human-Computer Interaction' volume that helped define the HCI literature.
Elected to the ACM SIGCHI CHI Academy for lifetime contributions to human-computer interaction.
Named ACM Fellow for contributions to HCI, computer graphics, and software visualization.
Received ACM SIGCHI Social Impact Award for work on technologies for aging gracefully.
Published 'Digital Dreams Have Become Nightmares: What We Must Do' with ACM on tech's societal risks and remedies.

name: Nicholas J. Belkin
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1942; University of Washington Slavic philology BA in 1968 (age ~26) is not a material CS/IR milestone. Library science degree 1970, University of London PhD 1977, and ASK (Anomalous State of Knowledge) work from ~1980 all occurred after 26. No material IR/CS milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Studied Slavic philology and then library science at the University of Washington (1968/1970), completed a London doctorate in 1977, and developed the influential ASK framework for information retrieval. Longtime Rutgers professor; SIGIR chair and ASIS&T president; Gerard Salton Award 2015.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia biography places birth in 1942 and field-defining ASK/IR work in the late 1970s–1980s. Undergraduate degree at ~26 was in Slavic philology, not a computing breakout. Career impact (Rutgers, SIGIR, Salton Award) is mid/late career.

name: Bing Xu
milestone_by_age_26: In 2014, at about age 23 (BEng BUPT 2009–2013; MSc Alberta beginning 2013), co-authored the seminal NeurIPS paper Generative Adversarial Nets with Goodfellow, Bengio, and others—one of the most cited papers in modern AI—and in 2015 co-created the MXNet deep-learning framework.
early_history_summary: Computer science BEng at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications (2009–2013), where he built early GPU infrastructure and ported Theano. Master's at University of Alberta under Dale Schuurmans (2013–2016) while contributing to GANs and DMLC systems (CXXNet, MXNet, XGBoost Python). Later engineering roles at GraphLab/Dato, Apple, Facebook/Meta, OctoML; founded HippoML (acquired by NVIDIA); NVIDIA Distinguished Engineer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: early GPU access, DMLC open source, GAN collaboration, Alberta advisor freedom, deep learning wave
evidence_summary: Education timeline on personal site (BUPT 2009–2013, Alberta 2013–2016) implies birth ~1991 for a standard Chinese CS path; even allowing ±2 years he was ≤26 for 2014–2015 milestones. GAN authorship is documented on the NeurIPS 2014 paper (Université de Montréal listing) and arXiv; MXNet authorship on the 2015 LearningSys/NIPS workshop paper. Family background is not documented. Strong open-source collaborator network (Tianqi Chen et al.) and the deep-learning structural wave were central.
starting_point: Not documented in detail; completed CS BEng at BUPT in Beijing (2009–2013) and moved to University of Alberta for graduate work—family/class origin not in reviewed sources.
current_position: Distinguished Engineer at NVIDIA (from 2024) after founding HippoML (acquired by NVIDIA); previously senior engineering roles at Meta/Facebook and Apple building GPU training and inference systems.

trajectory.event: Co-authored the original Generative Adversarial Nets paper (NeurIPS 2014), a foundational modern AI contribution.
Co-created MXNet, a major early deep-learning framework for heterogeneous distributed systems.
Joined GraphLab/Dato and then Apple; built early Apple GPU training systems after Dato's acquisition path.
Joined Facebook/Meta engineering, later creating AITemplate for multi-vendor GPU inference.
Founded HippoML as CEO, building high-performance GPU inference software.
HippoML acquired by NVIDIA; became NVIDIA Distinguished Engineer leading Pythonic AI systems work.

name: Hans-Juergen Boehm
milestone_by_age_26: Cornell PhD 1982 and Boehm–Demers–Weiser garbage collector (public release ~1988) are the career-defining contributions; without a confirmed birth year, and with secondary genealogy-style sources suggesting ~1951 birth (PhD ~age 31, GC ~age 37), no verified material milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Programming-language and systems researcher; PhD Cornell 1982; developed the widely used conservative Boehm GC for C/C++ with Demers and Weiser. Later University of Washington and Google Android runtime engineer.
evidence_summary: Wikidata/Google Research note Cornell PhD 1982; Boehm GC Wikipedia cites 1988 release. No reliable public birth year; GC fame is late-20s/30s+ on any reasonable estimate. Ineligible.

name: Chip Huyen
milestone_by_age_26: Born ~1990 (batch source; consistent with Stanford admit ~2014 at age ~24 after a multi-year gap). Created and taught Stanford CS20SI TensorFlow in Winter 2017 (age ~26–27 depending on birthday)—a strong early signal but age boundary is uncertain and the course is below the bar of a field-defining product/founding event. NVIDIA full-time (~2018–19), Designing ML Systems, Claypot AI founding/sale, and AI Engineering book fame arrived after 26. No clear, two-sourced material milestone strictly at age ≤26 found.
early_history_summary: Grew up in a rice-farming village in Vietnam; learned English largely on her own; rejected by Stanford out of high school, then spent ~3 years traveling and publishing Vietnamese travel books before reapplying successfully. Stanford CS BS/MS (~2018); student-initiated TensorFlow course; NVIDIA NeMo, Snorkel AI, Netflix RA; founded and sold Claypot AI; author of bestselling ML systems books.
family_context_summary: Grew up in a small rice-farming village in Vietnam; limited resources; English not learned as a child.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as tech/domain-adjacent; parents named in a Stanford post with nickname anecdote only.
evidence_summary: Personal site and interviews document Vietnam village origins, Stanford path, CS20SI Winter 2017, and later NVIDIA/Snorkel/Claypot/books. Because age at CS20 may have been 27 and broader fame is post-26, marked ineligible under the strict ≤26 material-milestone rule.

name: Angela Benton
milestone_by_age_26: In August 2007, at age 26, launched Black Web 2.0, the leading online publication covering Black innovators and digital strategy in technology, which established her as a go-to voice and platform-builder for underrepresented founders.
early_history_summary: Born May 22, 1981 in Chicago; raised largely in Northern Virginia. Had her first child at 16 while finishing high school early; graduated American InterContinental University magna cum laude (2004). Founded Black Web 2.0 in 2007, then NewME Accelerator (2011)—the first major Silicon Valley accelerator focused on minority founders—and later Streamlytics for ethical consumer data.
family_context_summary: Born in Chicago, raised in Northern Virginia; became a mother at 16 while still in high school and graduated early. Detailed parental occupations not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as tech-domain parents; no inherited Silicon Valley network.
primary_early_advantage_tags: teen parenthood, Black Web 2.0 platform, Web 2.0 wave, underrepresented-founder gap, online community
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and multiple profiles confirm birth May 22, 1981 and Black Web 2.0 launch August 2007 (age 26). Fast Company named her among Most Influential Women in Technology (2010). Teen motherhood and outsider path are documented in Inc and pioneer bios. No family capital or domain inheritance found; advantage stack is self-built distribution plus adversity catalyst on the Web 2.0 wave.
starting_point: Born May 22, 1981 in Chicago; raised in Northern Virginia; became a mother at 16 and finished high school early before college at American InterContinental University.
current_position: Founder and CEO/Executive Chairman of Streamlytics (ethical consumer-data platform); three-time founder known for NewME Accelerator and Black Web 2.0; essayist on AI, data ownership, and power.

trajectory.event: Launched Black Web 2.0, establishing the flagship online hub for Black tech entrepreneurship and digital culture coverage.
Named one of Fast Company's Most Influential Women in Technology for Black Web Media leadership.
Founded NewME Accelerator, the first Silicon Valley accelerator focused on underrepresented founders, featured in CNN's Black in America.
Featured Wall Street Journal essayist for the paper's 125th anniversary series on the future of entrepreneurship.
Founded Streamlytics to democratize ethical, consumer-owned streaming and media data; sold NewME the same year.
Named among Fast Company's Most Creative People in Business and Inc's Female Founders 100 for Streamlytics.

name: Alan C. Ashton
milestone_by_age_26: Born May 7, 1942; WordPerfect work began with a word-processor specification in 1977 (age ~35) and Satellite Software International incorporation in 1979 (age ~37). University of Utah computing/music study and BYU faculty path are post-26. No material founder/engineering fame milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born Salt Lake City; LDS missionary in Germany; University of Utah computing and music work in the early 1970s; BYU professor who co-created WordPerfect with student Bruce Bastian. Company became a dominant word-processor vendor; Ashton later co-founded Thanksgiving Point after Novell acquired WordPerfect.
family_context_summary: Grandson of LDS Church president David O. McKay; large family later (11 children with Karen Jackman Ashton).
parent_family_domain_summary: Prominent LDS family lineage; not a software-industry apprenticeship.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia documents birth May 7, 1942 and WordPerfect founding timeline in the late 1970s when Ashton was mid-30s. Early adulthood includes mission service and later academic work—not a ≤26 software breakout.
